Reddit (RDDT) stock fell 29.2% on October 30, 2026, during the first trading session after its fiscal Q3 2026 report. The S&P 500 lost 1.8% on the same day. This marks a steep fall following a quarter where revenue of $895 million came in about 2% above what analysts had expected. So what did Reddit tell investors that its results did not?

Reddit Warned Of A Drop In Daily Users

During the October 29 call, management said daily users could fall by a low double-digit percentage in the fourth quarter from a current base of 130 million. The warning came from search. Traffic that search engines send to Reddit fell meaningfully in fiscal Q3 2026, and the decline sped up late in the quarter. In October, those referrals dropped by more than 1 million a week on average, and management's estimate for users assumes that pace continues.

The results themselves held no surprise of that size. Earnings per share came in at $1.40, above the $1.33 analysts expected. Reddit's peers fell far less on the same day. Meta Platforms fell 1.5% and Alphabet fell 1.4%, while Pinterest, the weakest of the three peers, fell 2.8%. The fall was Reddit's own, not its industry's.

Is Reddit's Slowdown More Than One Quarter?

It is for sales growth. Reddit's revenue grew 69.1% from a year earlier in fiscal Q1 2026, a shade below the 69.7% posted in fiscal Q4 2025. Growth then slowed to 61.1% in fiscal Q2 2026 and to 53.0% in fiscal Q3 2026. Management expects growth to slow again in fiscal Q4 2026, forecasting revenue of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, or 38% to 42% growth. News reports on October 30 said that outlook was lower than expected. The traffic warning is new, but the slower growth is not.

Profitability is another matter. Reddit reported an operating margin of 29.2% in fiscal Q3 2026, compared with 23.7% a year earlier.

Management argued that Reddit is still growing where it counts: engagement from its app and logged-in users. About 80% of Reddit's monetization happens within that group, management said. The company added that Reddit is still a top search term in Google, and that Google is simply not sending people to Reddit the way it used to.

When Will Reddit's User Count Be Known?

The fiscal Q4 2026 results will be Reddit's first report since the warning. During that quarter, management plans to begin fully testing a logged-in-only version of Reddit in select markets outside the U.S. The company said the change would likely trade reach for engagement, noting that it will keep evaluating how it reports users.

The company's shares have lost 60.4% in the year-to-date period against the broader Zacks Computer & Technology sector's rise of 9.7%. It has also underperformed its peers in the digital advertising market, including companies like Pinterest PINS, Meta Platforms META and Alphabet GOOGL. All three companies lost 21.5%, 8.1% and 10.8% in the year-to-date period, respectively.

Despite the headwinds, Reddit's expanding advertising portfolio, strong engagement among logged-in and app users, gains in average revenue per user and growing adoption of AI-powered advertiser tools have been key growth catalysts. Rising advertiser spending, improved ad pricing and robust international demand have further supported its performance.

RDDT Benefits From Strong Advertising Portfolio

Reddit is benefiting from its expanding advertising portfolio, growing advertiser adoption and increasing demand for performance-driven marketing solutions. The company's investments in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning and advertising automation are strengthening monetization. In third-quarter 2026, advertising revenues surged 54% year over year to $847 million, driven by higher pricing and impressions. Click volume increased more than 50%, while conversion volume more than tripled, reflecting improving advertising effectiveness.

Reddit's AI-powered advertising solution, Reddit Max, is emerging as a key growth driver. The platform entered public beta in the third quarter, with advertiser adoption more than tripling sequentially. Enhanced machine-learning models, real-time signals and improved targeting capabilities are helping advertisers achieve better campaign performance. The company also expanded shopping capabilities to support up to 20 million products. Shopping and app-install advertising objectives each registered more than 95% year-over-year revenue growth in the third quarter of 2026, highlighting strong demand for lower-funnel solutions.

Reddit is also expanding its advertising opportunities through video, business-to-business (B2B) marketing and strategic partnerships. Video advertising revenues more than doubled year over year, supported by the introduction of a 15-second engaged video-view objective. Enhanced lead-generation tools and in-market audience targeting are strengthening Reddit's appeal among B2B advertisers.

Reddit's expanding advertising ecosystem, supported by integrations with Shopify, HubSpot, Smartly, Innovid and Skai, is improving accessibility for advertisers. Revenues from its Ads API ecosystem increased more than 45% sequentially in the third quarter of 2026. Improvements in personalized feeds, video experiences and community engagement are further strengthening user retention. These initiatives are expected to support sustainable advertising growth and higher average revenue per user.

title: Can Reddit Shrink to Grow?
detail:
Can Reddit Shrink to Grow?
Tim Beyers, The Motley Fool
Tue, November 3, 2026 at 7:38 AM EST 3 min read
RDDT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Team Rule Breakers

Shares of Reddit (NYSE:RDDT) were getting crushed in the pre-market Oct. 30, down over 21% as of this writing on Friday. That's an opportunity, Fools.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Before I get into why Reddit should interest you more, let's first discuss why institutions seem to want it less. It all comes down to growth.

Reddit is forecasting Q4 revenue will be up about 40% year-over-year, which is a marked slowdown from Q3's expectations-busting 53%. Adjusted EBITDA -- a key metric for the company -- is expected to be up about 51%, down from a 70% jump in the third quarter.

Forget for a moment that deceleration comes for every business. Algos still hate to see it. So do most investors.

Unfortunately, slowing growth is only part of what's causing Reddit's drawdown. Comments from co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman seem to have lit the match that's led to this morning's inferno.

"A key piece of work to retain new audiences is shifting Reddit to a logged-in-only experience. It's a big one for us, and it's a big one for me," Huffman wrote in the Q3 letter to shareholders.

Why the switch to logged-in only? Search traffic isn't helping Reddit as much as it used to. Pivoting to a more private experience forces Reddit to focus on the logged-in audience that drives 80% of the business. It's a risk, but there's logic to it.

Ask New York Times Co. (NYSE:NYT) whether it regrets going to a paywall-based business. Reddit demanding users log in is similar in that it may shrink the audience in the short term, but the long-term benefits of increased monetization could prove worth it.

Which brings us to why you may want to be interested. Even before Friday's action, Reddit was squarely on the way to generating $1 billion in annualized free cash flow. The shares trade for a 3.7% FCF yield, or about 27 times its real cash flow, as of this writing.

That might feel like a modest premium ... if Reddit hadn't spent the last three years more than doubling its cash from operations annually. There's a very real chance Reddit is going to keep growing cash flow at greater than 27% annually. Perhaps materially so. I sense a potential mispricing here.

Reddit's getting downvoted today. So be it. This stock story is far from over.

Key Takeaways

Reddit shares fell 34% in a week on weak fourth-quarter guidance and a warning that daily users could fall by a low-double-digit percentage.

CEO Steve Huffman blames AI Mode on Alphabet's Google, which keeps more searchers on Google itself.

Reddit is mostly losing logged-out visitors, while its logged-in users are still growing.

The stock looks cheap if logged-in users keep growing, and the fourth-quarter report is the next test.

Reddit (RDDT:NYSE) stock fell 34% in the five trading days through Monday, Nov. 2, after a third-quarter report that paired 53% revenue growth with a warning about its users.

The problem is Google. Alphabet (GOOG) is answering more searches with AI on its own pages, and fewer of those searchers reach Reddit.

A fine quarter with a short guide

Revenue rose to $895 million, with a 41% free cash flow margin. But fourth-quarter guidance of $1.00-$1.03 billion fell short of the $1.05 billion bar.

U.S. daily users fell 2% from a year earlier, and Reddit told shareholders search referral traffic was "down meaningfully in Q3, with the decline accelerating later in the quarter." If October's pace holds, total daily users could fall by a low-double-digit percentage this quarter.

Analysts still expect normalized EPS to more than double from 2025 to 2027:

Huffman blames AI Mode

On Reddit's Oct. 29 earnings call, founder and CEO Steve Huffman said Google is "crawling us as hard as ever," so the drop isn't about demand for Reddit's content. "The reality is the AI Mode does not drive traffic. Not for us, and not to anybody as far as I know."

Alphabet's stock fell 11.5% over the same five sessions, after its Oct. 28 report missed on earnings and showed free cash flow turning negative on heavy AI spending. Google's query growth was its fastest in five years, but Search & other revenue growth slowed to 12%, at $63.4 billion. More of those searches just end on Google.

So Huffman is betting on people who come to Reddit on purpose: "Google is teaching people that if you want to come to Reddit, you need to come to Reddit."

U.S. logged-out visitors fell 4% from a year earlier while logged-in users rose 1%, and logged-in and app users bring in over 80% of Reddit's monetization.

Key Takeaways

Snap shares fell 14% in a week as weak ad results and outlooks from Alphabet, Reddit and Pinterest hit social stocks, and Meta's settlement left Snap alone in a teen addiction trial.

Snap settled with the two teenage plaintiffs on Monday, taking the nearest legal risk off the table.

Snap reports third-quarter results on Nov. 4, against guidance of 1.70-1.74 billion of revenue and 300-350 million of adjusted EBITDA.

Most of the drop came from the group, so a quarter in the upper half of guidance would make Snap a buy.

Snap (SNAP:NYSE) stock is down 14% in the past week, mostly on other companies' bad news. Alphabet (GOOG), Reddit (RDDT:NYSE) and Pinterest (PINS:NYSE) all disappointed on ads, and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) settled out of a teen addiction trial, leaving Snap the only defendant until it settled on Monday.

Alphabet and Reddit spooked the ad crowd

Alphabet reported after the close on Oct. 28, and its third-quarter ad sales fell short of estimates. YouTube ads grew about 9% and Google Network was almost flat. That revived fears that AI is eating into digital advertising, and Alphabet is down 12% for the week.

A day later, Reddit warned that if falling referral traffic from Google search keeps up, its fourth-quarter daily users could drop by a low-double-digit percentage. It's down 34%.

That risk looks smaller for Snap. Snapchat is built around messaging friends rather than search, and its daily users rose 5% to 493 million in the second quarter.

Pinterest's news hits closer to home: it guided fourth-quarter revenue to $1.425- $1.475 billion, below the $1.52 billion analysts expected.

Snap ended up alone in court, then settled

Jury selection began in Los Angeles on Oct. 28, in what would have been Snap's first jury trial over claims that social media harms teens. Meta settled on Friday, and Snap followed on Monday, before opening statements, the plaintiffs' lawyers said.

More trials are coming, though. Snap CFO Doug Hott warned on the Aug. 3 call that they "may result in significant changes to our products and business practices." CEO Evan Spiegel has said ad revenue from impressions served to users under 18 isn't material. So the larger risk is design changes that could reduce engagement across all age groups, not a one-time payout.

StockStory's take

Reddit's third quarter results prompted a significant negative market reaction, despite year-on-year revenue growth and margin expansion. Management attributed the quarter's performance to robust advertising demand, with strong gains in both pricing and impressions, but also acknowledged that a sharp decline in search referral traffic—especially from Google—pressured user growth. CEO Steve Huffman highlighted that logged-in and app user engagement remained the primary revenue driver, stating, "We grew logged in and app dial sequentially. Together, these make up the vast majority of engagement and over 80% of the monetization on Reddit."

Looking ahead, Reddit's guidance reflects uncertainty stemming from ongoing declines in search referral traffic and a strategic shift towards a logged-in only platform experience. Management is focused on converting casual and search-referred users into engaged, logged-in app users through product enhancements and targeted marketing. Huffman explained, "Moving to primarily logged in will ensure our users have the best Reddit experience possible and can find the content and communities most relevant to them." While the team sees opportunity to further close the monetization gap with larger social platforms, they acknowledged that transitioning engagement sources introduces risks to future growth.

title: These 2 Tech Stocks Both Fell 29% on Friday. Are They Buying Opportunities Now?
detail:
These 2 Tech Stocks Both Fell 29% on Friday. Are They Buying Opportunities Now?
Matt Frankel, CFP®, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 2:24 PM EST 5 min read

RDDT
^IXIC
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Friday was a rough day for tech stocks in general. The Nasdaq Composite fell by nearly 3%. But two stocks in particular had days that will go down in history after issuing their latest earnings reports.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) fell by nearly 29% on Friday, erasing roughly $140 billion in market value. It was the chipmaker's worst day since July 1974. Reddit (NYSE:RDDT) also fell by about 29% after its earnings report, its worst day since it went public in 2024.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

To be clear, neither company had a bad quarter. Intel beat its own forecast, and Reddit grew its revenue by more than half. Here's what went wrong for each, and why the two problems are more connected than they might seem.

Intel had a good quarter and a bad forecast

Intel's third-quarter revenue grew 21% year over year to $16.5 billion, and adjusted earnings per share of $0.52 came in well above the company's own guidance. Its data center and AI segment was the standout, with revenue up 78% to $7.3 billion. CFO David Zinsner called it the company's strongest data center growth in 15 years.

The problem was the outlook. Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, well below the roughly $17 billion analysts expected. Management also expects adjusted EPS of just $0.25, while analysts were looking for about $0.43. Intel's adjusted gross margin is expected to fall to about 38% from 44.1% in the third quarter.

The biggest culprit is the PC market. AI data centers are absorbing so many memory chips that laptop and desktop prices are rising, and Intel now expects PC shipments to fall about 12% this year and another 10% in 2027. An accident at its factory in Israel will also cost roughly $300 million of fourth-quarter revenue.

It's also worth noting how much optimism was already priced in. Intel's stock nearly quadrupled from the start of the year to its June high, and even after Friday it's still up more than 70% in 2026.

Reddit grew fast, but its traffic is slipping

Reddit's third-quarter revenue rose 53% to $895 million, ahead of analysts' estimates, and adjusted EBITDA jumped 70% to $402 million. By most measures, it was an excellent quarter.

However, management said search engine traffic fell meaningfully, and the decline accelerated as the quarter went on. According to CEO Steve Huffman, search referrals fell by more than 1 million per week on average in October, and Google's AI Mode "does not drive traffic." U.S. daily users slipped 2% to 50.7 million, and Reddit warned that total daily users could fall by a low-double-digit percentage this quarter. Its profit guidance also came in a bit below analysts' estimates.

While we enjoy listening to the management's commentary, our favorite part of earnings calls is the analyst questions. Those are unscripted and can often highlight topics that management teams would rather avoid or topics where the answer is complicated. Here is what has caught our attention.

Our top 5 analyst questions from Reddit's Q3 earnings call

Benjamin Black (Deutsche Bank) asked about the rationale and expected impact of moving to a logged-in only experience. CEO Steve Huffman clarified that this transition aims to improve engagement and ad targeting but acknowledged trade-offs in reach, while COO Jen Wong highlighted that over 80% of monetization already comes from this user base.

Josh Beck (Raymond James) inquired about the drivers behind the decline in Google traffic and the scaling potential of paid user marketing. Huffman attributed traffic drops primarily to AI-driven search changes, while Wong said early app install campaigns show promising retention rates but are still small in scale.

John Colantuoni (Jefferies) questioned the extent and permanence of the logged-in only shift and engagement trends. Huffman said the transition is a test but will be permanent, with engagement improvements among app users partially offsetting overall traffic declines.

Tom Champion (Piper) asked if the current strategic environment resembles past inflection points and about future ARPU growth. Huffman referenced past periods of change and said product improvements will help drive daily habits, while Vollero pointed to the unique commercial potential of Reddit's user base for further ARPU gains.

Jason Helfstein (Oppenheimer) sought clarity on how to model user monetization after the shift and whether the platform will become less accessible to web scrapers. Huffman responded that testing will inform boundaries and confirmed that the move will make Reddit harder to scrape, protecting valuable data.
